I'm going to be honest about something most women on Wegovy® and Ozempic® don't want to admit out loud.

The only thing that fixed my constipation wasn't anything my prescriber recommended. It wasn't anything the pharmacist suggested. It wasn't anything I found in the supplement aisle. It wasn't the $40 "gentle" laxative tea my well-meaning sister mailed me. It wasn't the prescription Senna squares my GP wrote up after my third complaint.

I tried all of it. None of it worked.

If you're on Wegovy®, Ozempic®, Mounjaro®, Zepbound®, or Foundayo™ and you've spent the last three months building a graveyard of laxatives in your bathroom cabinet — read this. The reason none of it has worked has nothing to do with you. It has to do with what your medication is actually doing inside your body.

I started Wegovy® eleven months ago. By month three I was down 22 pounds. By month seven, 41. I should have been thrilled. Instead I was sitting on my bathroom floor at 6 AM crying because I hadn't gone in eight days.

Here's what I tried. In order. Because I want you to recognize yourself somewhere on this list.

Miralax. $15. Drank it for two weeks. The first three days I went a little. Then it stopped — but the bloating was worse. My pants didn't fit by Friday afternoon. My stomach looked seven months pregnant.

Fiber gummies. $20. Took them for a month. Stomach got harder, not softer. I'd lie down at night and you could see the outline of where the food was sitting in my abdomen. It sat in my gut like a rock.

That "gentle" laxative tea. $40. A box. Forty dollars for a small box of tea bags that did nothing. I threw the rest of the box in the trash.

Dulcolax. $13. Got the cramps. Got the 4 AM agony. Did not get the relief.

Prescription senna squares. Miserable. Embarrassing to ask my doctor for. Cramps so bad I missed work twice. And I still couldn't go.

Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle. $12. Did absolutely nothing. (I learned later why — your body absorbs about 4% of magnesium oxide. The label said 500mg. I was getting maybe 20mg of usable magnesium per dose.)

Probiotic. $40. Marketed for "digestive support." Six weeks. No change.

A "GLP-1 daily" multivitamin from Amazon. $42. Came in two days. Took it for two months. If anything, the bloating got worse.

I added it up one morning. Over $180 in three months on supplements and laxatives that did nothing or made me feel worse. I had a discontinuation appointment scheduled with my prescriber for that Wednesday. I was going to throw away my 41 pounds because I couldn't take another night of this.

Then my niece — who's a pharmacy tech in Phoenix — sent me a 12-minute video that explained why every single thing on that list was the wrong mechanism for what's actually happening on a GLP-1.

It changed everything.

Here's what no one had explained to me before:

Your GLP-1 medication works by slowing your gastric emptying by 50% or more. That's the therapeutic mechanism. That's why you stop being hungry. That's why I lost 41 pounds.

But the same slowed motility doesn't stop at your stomach. It runs your entire digestive system. Stool sits longer. Dries out. Compacts. Food in the stomach for twice as long as it should be ferments — that's where the sulfur burps come from, by the way. Bacteria breaking down food in a stomach that should have already emptied.

This is why every single product on my list failed for the same reason:

Fiber doesn't work on a GLP-1 because fiber adds bulk that needs gut motility to push it through. My motility was being intentionally suppressed by my Wegovy®. I was adding bulk to a system that couldn't move bulk. It just makes a bigger backup.

Stimulant laxatives don't work because they trigger contractions that my Wegovy® was designed to suppress. The two drugs fought each other inside my body. I felt the cramping. I didn't get the relief. The GLP-1 wins every single time. Dulcolax, Senna, that "gentle" tea — same mechanism, same failure.

Magnesium oxide doesn't work because oxide is the cheapest, least bioavailable form. 4% of it gets absorbed. The label was lying to me with technical truth.

Probiotics didn't work because the problem wasn't my microbiome. The problem was upstream of it.

I needed something designed for Ozempic® constipation. Not a normal one.

The video walked through what actually works:

Magnesium glycinate — pulls water into the gut osmotically. It doesn't require contractions. It works WITH a slowed system instead of fighting it. Bioavailable form your body actually absorbs.

Ginger root extract standardized to 5% gingerols — a natural prokinetic. Helps your stomach empty so food doesn't sit and rot. Stops the fermentation that causes the sulfur burps. Doesn't force contractions, so it doesn't fight your medication.

Methylcobalamin B12 — the active form, not the cheap synthetic. Addresses the energy depletion that comes from reduced calorie intake and impaired absorption.

Three nutrients. Right forms. Designed for the slowed-on-purpose mechanism your medication creates.

The video pointed me to a small brand called GLP-1 SOS™. Magnesium glycinate verified at the labeled dose. Ginger root standardized to 5.1% gingerols by HPLC. Methylcobalamin B12 in the active form. Manufactured in an FDA-registered facility in Utah. Third-party Certificate of Analysis on every batch.

It costs $24.99 for a 30-day supply.

I was twelve hours from canceling a $1,400-a-month medication. Twenty-five dollars to try one more thing wasn't a risk. It was less than half of what I'd spent on the laxative tea alone.

I cancelled the discontinuation appointment that morning. I ordered GLP-1 SOS™ that afternoon.

Day 1: nothing.

Day 2: nothing.

Day 3: nothing. I started to think it was another lie.

Day 4: I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. Just relief.

48 hours after my first dose, the sulfur burps stopped completely. By week two I was sleeping through the night without 4 AM cramps. By week three I had energy at 3 PM for the first time since I'd started Wegovy®. By week four my husband Tom and I went out to dinner and I sat for two hours and I never once excused myself.

I'm still on Wegovy®. Still down to 158. A1C 5.3 — best it's been in twenty years.

It's been four months now. I'm going like clockwork. No cramping. No bloating. No sulfur burps. No bathroom emergencies. No more mornings on the floor.

If you're sitting in your bathroom right now reading this with a graveyard of failed laxatives on your counter — please hear me. Save your money. Stop buying the next $20, $40, $90 product that's the same wrong mechanism as the previous eight.

You don't need a different brand. You don't need a different dose. You need a different mechanism — one designed for Ozempic® constipation, not a normal one.

That's GLP-1 SOS™. 27,000+ people on Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®, Zepbound®, and Foundayo™ are on it now. Made in the USA. FDA-registered facility. Third-party tested. 60-day money-back guarantee. $24.99 for a 30-day supply.

Her name is Helen. She's 62. And she almost quit her Ozempic® last month over something nobody warned her about.

When Helen started Ozempic® eight months ago, her endocrinologist talked about appetite suppression. Talked about A1C. Talked about gradual titration. Drew her a chart of expected weight loss.

What he didn't talk about was what the medication was actually doing inside her gut.

Because Ozempic® changes your gut more than you think.

By month four, Helen was down 27 pounds and thrilled. By month five, she was sitting on her bathroom floor at 6 AM crying because she hadn't gone in eight days.

If you're on Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®, Zepbound®, or Foundayo™ — read every word of this. Because what happened to Helen is happening to thousands of women on these medications right now, and the reason none of the things she tried worked has nothing to do with her body and everything to do with the mechanism nobody bothered to explain.

Helen tried everything.

Miralax. Two capfuls every morning. The first three days, she went a little. Then it stopped — and the bloating was worse.

Dulcolax stool softeners. Two boxes. Cramping at 4 AM that woke her husband Frank. Still didn't go.

Fiber gummies. Forty bucks a bottle. After two weeks, her stomach looked seven months pregnant. She had to buy "transition pants" two sizes up just to button them.

Senna at night. "Gentle laxative tea" from the wellness store, $42. Probiotic capsules her sister mailed her. Prune juice. Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle.

She'd spent over $300 in three months on supplements and laxatives.

Some of them actually made the bloating worse.

She went to her primary care doctor. He suggested more fiber.

She went to her gastroenterologist. He ordered a colonoscopy. $2,800. Clean. "Within normal range."

She brought a printed list to her next appointment with a clipboard of every product she'd tried, every dose, every duration. Her doctor never explained why none of them had worked. He told her some patients just don't tolerate GLP-1 medications well, and they could talk about discontinuation.

Helen went home and pulled up the discontinuation form. The 27 pounds were going to go back. So was the better A1C. So was the energy that had let her play with her grandkids again.

Then her daughter-in-law sent her a video that explained the one thing nobody else had.

Ozempic® works by slowing gastric emptying by 50% or more. That's the therapeutic mechanism. That's why she stopped being hungry. That's why the weight came off. That's why her A1C dropped.

But the same slowed motility doesn't stop at the stomach. It slows the entire digestive system. Stool sits longer. Dries out. Compacts. Food that should empty in two hours sits for four. By the time it gets to where it needs to be, the body can't push it out without help.

And here's the part nobody had told her — the part that explained why every product on her bathroom counter had failed:

Regular laxatives add MORE bulk to a system that's already stuck.

Fiber works by adding bulk that gut motility moves through. But on Ozempic®, the motility is being intentionally suppressed. So fiber adds bulk to a system that can't move bulk. The bloating gets worse, not better. That's why the fiber gummies and the Metamucil and the prescription bulk-formers had all made her feel like her stomach was about to explode.

Stimulant laxatives — Dulcolax, Senna, Bisacodyl — work by forcing intestinal muscles to contract. But on Ozempic®, those exact contractions are being suppressed. So the laxative and the medication fight inside the body. The cramping is the conflict. The lack of relief is the GLP-1 winning. Every. Single. Time.

Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle? 4% bioavailable. Helen had been getting maybe 20mg of usable magnesium per dose, even though the label said 500mg.

The "GLP-1 multivitamin" from Amazon? Under-dosed. Wrong forms. Useless.

What she needed was something specifically designed for a slow GLP-1 gut. Not a normal one.

That's where GLP-1 SOS™ came in.

The video walked Helen through the formulation. Three nutrients. Right forms. Built for the slowed-on-purpose mechanism the medication creates.

Magnesium glycinate — pulls water INTO the gut osmotically. Doesn't require contractions. Works WITH the slowed system instead of fighting it. Gently pulls water into the gut without adding bulk.

Ginger root extract standardized to 5% gingerols — natural prokinetic. Gets the stomach MOVING again. Helps the stomach empty so food doesn't sit and ferment. Stops the sulfur burps. Doesn't force contractions, so it doesn't fight the medication.

Methylcobalamin B12 — the active form, not the cheap synthetic. Addresses the energy depletion from reduced calorie intake.

Made in the USA. FDA-registered facility. Third-party Certificate of Analysis on every batch. Two capsules with dinner. That's it.

Helen ordered it that afternoon.

Day 1: nothing.

Day 2: nothing.

Day 3: nothing. She almost convinced herself it was another bottle for the trash.

Day 4: she went. Gently. No straining. No urgency. Just relief.

48 hours after her first dose, the sulfur burps stopped completely. By week two she was sleeping through the night. By week three her energy came back at 3 PM for the first time in months. By week four she had Frank and the grandkids over for Sunday dinner and didn't excuse herself once in three hours.

It's been four months now.

She's still on Ozempic®. Still down to 152. A1C 5.3 — best she's had since 2009.

Like clockwork. Just normal.

She tore up the discontinuation form. She threw away the laxative graveyard from her bathroom counter. She hasn't been constipated since week one.

If you're sitting in your bathroom right now reading this with the same graveyard of failed laxatives Helen had — please hear this:

It's not your body. It's not your willpower. It's not "you just don't tolerate the medication." It's the mechanism nobody screened you for, and it has a name, and it has a $24 answer that's not on your prescriber's protocol because the protocols were written before these medications existed.

You don't need a different brand. You don't need a different dose. You need a different mechanism — built specifically for a slow GLP-1 gut. Not a normal one.

That's GLP-1 SOS™. 27,000+ people on Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®, Zepbound®, and Foundayo™ are on it now. Made in the USA. FDA-registered facility. Third-party tested. 60-day money-back guarantee. $24.99 for a 30-day supply.

You're already paying $1,000-1,400/month for the medication. $24.99/month to actually function on it isn't a stretch.

Ditch the laxatives. Finally feel normal on your GLP-1.

GLP-1 SOS Supplements
Sponsored
I have a crumpled pharmacy receipt on my kitchen table that adds up to $140.92.

Eight items. Every single one I bought because someone — my prescriber, a Facebook group, an Instagram ad, my well-meaning sister — told me it would help with my Wegovy® side effects.

Miralax. Twenty-four ninety-nine.
Fiber gummies. Nineteen ninety-nine.
Dulcolax. Twelve ninety-nine.
Probiotic capsules. Thirty-nine ninety-nine.
Ginger tea. Eight ninety-nine.
Senna at night. Fourteen ninety-nine.
Prune juice. Six ninety-nine.
Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle. Eleven ninety-nine.

Not a single one worked.

I'm not telling you this to complain about the pharmacy. I'm telling you because I see thousands of women on Wegovy®, Ozempic®, Mounjaro®, Zepbound®, and Foundayo™ standing in the same aisle right now buying the exact same eight items I bought, and I don't want one more of you to spend the next $140 the way I spent mine.

If you're on a GLP-1 medication right now and you've been cycling through fiber and laxatives for weeks or months wondering which one will finally work — read every word of this. Because the answer is in here, and it isn't another bottle of fiber.

My name is Sarah K. I'm 58. I started Wegovy® last September at 219 pounds. By April I was 178. Forty-one pounds. The first time my husband Dan saw me in jeans I hadn't fit into in nine years, he started crying.

I should have been thrilled. Instead I was crying in my bathroom because I hadn't gone in seven days.

The cramps from Dulcolax. The bloating from psyllium. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs and made the woman next to me at coffee visibly recoil. The 3 PM exhaustion that flattened me onto my couch like I was twenty years older than I am. The brain fog so thick I forgot my own granddaughter's name at her dance recital.

I was watching myself disappear inside a body I'd just spent eight months earning back from my own metabolism.

So I went to the pharmacy.

The receipt grew, week by week.

Week 1: Miralax. Two cap-fulls every morning. For three days I went. Then it stopped — but with worse bloating than before.

Week 2: Add fiber gummies. Choked them down with a glass of water. Bloating worse.

Week 3: Add Dulcolax at night. Got the cramps. Got the 4 AM agony. Did not get the relief.

Week 4: Add probiotic — "maybe it's your microbiome." Forty dollars. Nothing.

Week 5: Add ginger tea — "ginger helps digestion." Nothing.

Week 6: Add Senna. Add prune juice. Add a magnesium supplement from the supplement aisle.

Week 7: I added it all up on the back of an envelope. $140.92. I cried at the kitchen table.

I called my prescriber and said I was going to discontinue. The video appointment was scheduled for that Tuesday. I had the form half-filled out next to the pile of bottles.

That same week, my friend Marlene quit her Ozempic® for the exact same reasons. Marlene is 60. She'd lost 47 pounds. She told me on the phone, sobbing, that she couldn't take another night of bathroom cramping and another morning of pretending she didn't smell like rotten eggs at her grandson's basketball game. She quit. By month three she'd gained back 19 pounds. By month seven, 43.

I sat at my kitchen table the night before my discontinuation appointment, looking at the $140.92 receipt and listening to Marlene's voicemail, and I thought: I'm about to do exactly what she did, in exactly the same order, and the only difference will be that I waste another $140 the same way she did before I quit.

That night, instead of submitting the form, I started reading.

I read every comment under every "I quit my Wegovy®" post I could find. I read clinical articles I half-understood. I read a 14-page review on what GLP-1 medications actually do to the digestive tract. By 3 AM, the entire $140 receipt had stopped being eight separate failed products and had become the same product, eight times.

Here's what I finally understood — and what nobody who'd sold me anything on that receipt had bothered to explain:

Your medication is intentionally slowing your gastric emptying by 50% or more. That's the therapeutic mechanism. That's why you stop being hungry. That's why you lose the weight.

But the same slowed motility runs the entire GI tract. Stool sits longer. Dries. Compacts. Food in the stomach for twice as long ferments — that's the sulfur burps. Bacteria breaking down food in a stomach that should have already emptied.

This is the part where every single item on my $140 receipt failed for the same reason:

Fiber doesn't work because fiber adds bulk that needs gut motility to push it through. My motility was being intentionally suppressed by my Wegovy®. I was adding bulk to a system that couldn't move bulk. Bloating got worse, not better. Metamucil, fiber gummies, prune juice — same mechanism, same failure.

Stimulant laxatives don't work because they trigger contractions that my Wegovy® was designed to suppress. The two drugs fought inside me. I felt the cramping. I didn't get the relief. The GLP-1 wins every time. Dulcolax, Senna — same mechanism, same failure.

Probiotics didn't work because the problem wasn't my microbiome. The problem was upstream of it.

Ginger tea didn't work because brewed tea has a tiny fraction of the gingerols you'd need to actually shift gastric motility. The active compound was almost absent in the bottle.

Magnesium oxide didn't work because oxide is the cheapest, least bioavailable form. My body absorbs about 4% of it. The label said 500mg. I was getting maybe 20mg of usable magnesium per dose.

Why doesn't Miralax work on Ozempic®?

I'm asking because I spent four months not knowing the answer, and I almost threw away 30 pounds of progress trying to find it.

And once you understand it, the whole bathroom counter starts making sense.

Read every word.

I started Ozempic® nine months ago. By month four I was down 30 pounds. By month five I was sitting on my bathroom floor at 6 AM with my hands covering my face, trying to figure out how to keep both — the medication that was working AND a working digestive system.

The constipation started slowly. Three days. Four days. Five days. Then six and seven days at a stretch.

The bloating was unreal. I'd lift my pajama shirt in front of my bathroom mirror and my stomach looked like a balloon. I had to buy "transition pants" two sizes up just for the days my regular jeans wouldn't button.

Miralax. Two capfuls every morning. It didn't work.

Fiber gummies. Forty bucks a bottle. It didn't work.

Dulcolax stool softeners. Cramping at 4 AM. It didn't work.

Prescription senna. It didn't work.

Prune juice. Stool softener tea. Phillips Milk of Magnesia. Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle. Probiotic gummies. A "GLP-1 daily" multivitamin from Amazon for $42.

Nothing worked.

I lined them all up on my kitchen table one afternoon and counted nine products. Over $250 in three months on supplements and laxatives that did nothing or made me feel worse.

I had a discontinuation appointment booked with my prescriber for that Friday. I was going to throw away 30 pounds of progress because I couldn't take another night of cement-belly and 4 AM cramping.

That same week, my friend Karen came over for our monthly coffee.

We've known each other since our kids were in elementary school. She's been on Mounjaro® for a year. She'd lost 35 pounds and looked great — and unlike me, she didn't look exhausted.

I told her everything. The discontinuation appointment. The graveyard of laxatives. The fact that I was about to quit.

She set her coffee down and reached into her purse.

Here's what nobody had explained to me in nine months on the medication:

Ozempic® works by slowing down your entire digestive system. That's the therapeutic mechanism. That's how it kills your appetite. That's why I lost 30 pounds.

But the same slowed motility doesn't stop at your stomach. Everything gets stuck. Stool sits longer. Dries out. Compacts. Food in the stomach for twice as long ferments — that's where the sulfur burps come from.

Now here's why every product on my counter failed for the same reason:

Regular laxatives add bulk to a system that's already stuck.

Fiber works by adding bulk that needs gut motility to push it through. But on Ozempic®, motility is being intentionally suppressed by the medication. Adding bulk to a system that can't move bulk just makes the backup BIGGER. That's why the fiber gummies made my bloating worse — they were doing exactly what they're designed to do, but in the wrong body for that mechanism.

Stimulant laxatives — Dulcolax, Senna, Bisacodyl, that "gentle" laxative tea — work by forcing intestinal contractions. But on Ozempic®, those exact contractions are being suppressed. The two drugs fight inside you. The cramping is the conflict. The lack of relief is the GLP-1 winning. Every. Single. Time.

Magnesium oxide from the supplement aisle? Your body absorbs about 4% of it. The label said 500mg. I was getting maybe 20mg of usable magnesium per dose. Useless.

The "GLP-1 daily" Amazon multivitamin? Under-dosed. Wrong forms. Filler-heavy. Useless.

That's why Miralax doesn't work on Ozempic®. Same reason fiber doesn't work. Same reason Dulcolax doesn't work. Same reason prescription senna doesn't work. Same reason the magnesium aisle doesn't work.

They're all built for a normal-motility body. You don't have a normal-motility body anymore. You have a slowed-on-purpose body. The interventions have to match.

Magnesium glycinate — pulls water INTO the gut osmotically, without requiring contractions. Doesn't add bulk. Works WITH your slow system instead of fighting it. Softens everything gently.

Ginger root extract standardized to 5% gingerols — gets the stomach actually moving again. Natural prokinetic. Helps the stomach empty so food doesn't sit and ferment. Doesn't force contractions, so it doesn't fight the medication. Peristalsis kicks back in. Like it's supposed to.

I'm still on Ozempic®. Still down to 167 pounds — the scale moved another 8 pounds in the four weeks I've been on the supplement, after sitting completely flat for two months.

And I'm still losing weight. Not because the supplement is making me lose weight — but because I didn't quit my Ozempic®.
